items.text: Autistic burnout isn't a motivation problem. It's a capacity problem. The difference matters: rest alone won't fix capacity collapse. Neither will trying harder.
items.rationale: Delivers the core reframe from Angle 1 in three declarative beats — names the misread, corrects the mechanism, closes the loop. No sentiment, no throat-clearing. Cuts the shame at the root.

items.text: Doctors called it depression. Friends called it laziness. It was neither. Autistic burnout is what happens when your nervous system runs out of capacity — not will.
items.rationale: Opens with the misdiagnosis experience late-identified autistic adults will recognize instantly, then names the corrective frame without moralizing. Scene-setting plus pivot — different shape from post 1 despite shared Angle 1 source.

items.text: For AuDHD brains with a PDA profile, 'just do it' doesn't build momentum. It registers as a threat. The anxiety goes up, not down. That's not weakness — it's mechanism.
items.rationale: Delivers the backfire logic from Angle 2 in a causality chain short enough to screenshot. 'PDA profile' used deliberately rather than 'PDA diagnosis' to stay accurate to how the term circulates in community and clinical writing.
items.sensitivity_flag: PDA is not formally recognized in DSM-5. 'PDA profile' framing is used deliberately. Mechanism claim is drawn from community and clinical writing, not a controlled RCT — flag if clinical sourcing is requested.

items.text: A 2026 study found sensory over-reactivity — not anxiety, not intolerance of uncertainty — was the only factor that uniquely distinguished PDA profiles in autistic kids. That changes where you look first.
items.rationale: Leads with the counterintuitive finding from the peer-reviewed Research in Autism study (n=795, ages 4–17). Posts the genuine surprise, then implies practical utility in one sentence rather than spelling it out. Claim is specific and defensible.
items.sensitivity_flag: Study population is children ages 4–17; post specifies 'autistic kids,' which is accurate to the research scope. Do not extrapolate to adults without additional sourcing.

items.text: What looks like defiance in a PDA child is a nervous system protecting something it treats as survival: autonomy. The adult's job shifts from 'gain control' to 'create safety.'
items.rationale: Gives parents the gut-level frame shift from Angle 4 in two sentences. Names the mechanism, then immediately repoints the adult's role — practical redirect embedded in the reframe. Validates the child without dismissing the adult's struggle.
items.sensitivity_flag: PDA recognition varies by country and clinical framework. 'PDA child' is community shorthand; no diagnostic claim is made. Sensitivity is low but worth noting for international audiences.

items.text: If getting your diagnosis brought up grief before relief, you're not doing it wrong. The rage, the mourning — they're for a younger you who deserved a map and didn't get one.
items.rationale: Addresses the under-discussed grief arc from Angle 5 without pivoting to inspiration framing. Opens with the feeling, names what's underneath, closes in a way that honors the emotion rather than rushing past it. No cure framing, no pity.

items.text: 82% of employed neurodivergent adults say stigma forces them to mask at work. That's a second, invisible job — no job description, no pay, no end time.
items.rationale: Grounds the masking-as-labor insight from Angle 6 in a defensible statistic, then makes the mechanism vivid with the 'second job' metaphor. Concise; the image does the emotional work without requiring explanation.
items.sensitivity_flag: 82% figure is from a Frontiers in Psychology 2026 study as cited in Forbes — not a nationally representative probability sample. Stat is defensible but should not be presented as population prevalence if challenged.

items.text: 45% of neurodivergent employees report exhaustion at work always or often. If your company issued an RTO mandate this year, what accommodations did they offer — and did any of them actually help?
items.rationale: Grounds the RTO discussion-opener from Angle 7 in a concrete stat before asking the question, so the ask feels earned rather than abstract. Genuine experience-gathering framing, not outrage bait. Stat-first structure differentiates from the accommodation question post.
items.sensitivity_flag: 45% exhaustion stat is cited via HR Magazine; verify the underlying study source if challenged. Comparative 30% neurotypical figure omitted for space — present if asked to substantiate.

items.text: Rest doesn't fix AuDHD burnout alone. But it also doesn't need to be earned first. Start with rest. Then reduce demands. You don't have to justify either.
items.rationale: Holds both stuck points from Angle 8 in one tight post — 'rest alone isn't enough' and 'rest doesn't need to be earned.' Two-part structure, plain language, no moralizing. Useful without being prescriptive or implying a recovery protocol.

items.text: What accommodation would actually change your workday — not in theory, but right now? Written instructions instead of verbal, async check-ins, somewhere quiet to reset? Genuinely curious what's working.
items.rationale: Surfaces the real-world accommodation gap from Angle 9 as community intelligence-gathering. Two concrete examples lower the threshold for responding without prescribing answers. Direct question; no stat required as a lead-in here.

items.text: Many autistic people have reduced interoceptive awareness — the body's early signals for fatigue and overwhelm don't register clearly. Burnout arrives as a cliff, not a slope. That's neurology, not neglect.
items.rationale: Names the interoception mechanism from Angle 10 in a way that reframes a common self-blame story. 'Cliff not a slope' is a vivid, accurate image. 'Many' is the correct hedge — interoception differences vary across individuals. Closes with reframe, not prescription.

items.text: ADHD avoidance = dopamine deficit. PDA avoidance = autonomy threat. Same surface, different engine. They need different responses — which means 'try harder' is the wrong tool for both.
items.rationale: Distils the mechanism distinction from Angle 2 into its sharpest form. Equation format is punchy and scannable. Closes with a practical implication without prescribing a specific intervention. Differentiated from post 3 by framing both mechanisms side-by-side rather than focusing on backfire alone.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'ADHD avoidance = dopamine deficit' is a mechanistic simplification accurate for a 280-char post but reductive of the fuller executive-function picture. Flag if readers with clinical training push back. PDA not DSM-recognized; used here as accepted community shorthand.
